Vanessa: Hey, Sally! It's great to see you! It's been a while since we grabbed a coffee.
Sally: Yes, I've missed our yak sessions and we haven't been out dancing for ages. I have something I really need to run by you.
Vanessa: Oh ... it sounds like you may have a decision to make.
Sally: Yeah, there's something I've been mulling over and I think you may be able to help me.
Vanessa: Well, I think I know you inside and out and I could definitely give you some pointers.

Sally: That's true. It seems like you know me really well. We spend a lot of time hanging out and I really value your opinion.
Vanessa: Wow! This sounds serious! You must be contemplating a big change.
Sally: It's something I've been thinking about and it could be really exciting for me.
Vanessa: I'm intrigued! And a bit alarmed. Tell me! What's going on?
Sally: Okay, I'll tell you what I'm considering and I think you could help me figure out if it's a good idea.

Vanessa: Okay, sounds good. We'll hash out the details together!
Sally: I feel like I can count on you to help me make this decision. But I need to ask you if you can keep my idea to yourself for now. I don't want anyone else to know until I've made my final decision.
Vanessa: Of course! I can keep a secret!

Explaining Your Opinions
When you explain your opinion, you use the Simple Present or the Simple Past. You can use verbs like think, or seem to express opinions.
To express opinions, you can use phrases like:

• I think ...
  • He seems ...
  • It looks like ...

Modal Verbs for Speculating
When you speculate about something, you are making a guess based on what you know about the situation.
You can show you are speculating about something by using a modal, like must, might, may or could.
The modal verb is followed by the main verb in the base form. You do not use “to”. Do not add “ing”, “ed”, or “s” to the verb.

Example:
It could be really exciting for me.
These are formal structures.
It sounds like you may have a decision to make.
I think you may be able to help me.

to inform someone about a situation so that they can give an opinion about it
(phrasal verb)

These are words you use to talk about social activities and decision-making.
to mull over
to reflect about something over a period of time
(verb)
Example: There's something I've been mulling over and I think you may be able to help me.
engenn8le18ob01aud02
inside and out
to have a deep knowledge about something or someone
(expression)
Example: I think I know you inside and out and I could definitely give you some pointers.
engenn8le18ob01aud03
yak session
a chat or talk that takes a long period of time
(noun)
Example: I've missed our yak sessions and we haven't been out dancing for ages.
engenn8le18ob01aud04
to value
to consider something or someone is worthy and important
(verb)
Example: We spend a lot of time hanging out and I really value your opinion.
engenn8le18ob01aud05
to contemplate
to consider something as possible in the future
(verb)
Example: This sounds serious! You must be contemplating a big change.
engenn8le18ob01aud06
intrigued
interested and wanting to know about something or someone
(adjective)
Example: I'm intrigued! Tell me! What's going on?
engenn8le18ob01aud07
alarmed
feeling frightened about a situation
(adjective)
Example: I'm feeling a bit alarmed. Tell me! What's going on?
engenn8le18ob01aud08
to figure out
to solve or understand a situation
(phrasal verb)
Example: I think you could help me figure out if it's a good idea.
engenn8le18ob01aud09
to hash out
to discuss a plan in order to get to an agreement
(phrasal verb)
Example: We'll hash out the details together!
